items.title: A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
items.summary: The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.
items.full_text: The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow. To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees. Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years. The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships. Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries. While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner. items.title: She Is Rewriting Mexico’s Ballads, One Woman’s Story at a Time
items.summary: Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.
items.full_text: Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba. Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers. Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife. “I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!” On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.

items.title: They Left Iran, but Now the Regime Is Seizing Their Assets to Silence Them
items.summary: The Iranian authorities are pursuing diaspora dissidents and journalists, extending the government’s repressive apparatus far beyond its borders.
items.full_text: The retired couple in Iran first realized that something was wrong when their bank cards stopped working in early May. After inquiring with the authorities, they discovered that their assets had been frozen by order of the country’s intelligence ministry. The couple learned, eventually, that they were being punished for the actions of their daughter Noushin Najafiragheb, who lived in Europe — specifically, for her social media posts opposing the Iranian government, according to another daughter, Mehrnoush Najafiragheb. Across Iran, the government has used asset seizures as punishment for actions taken abroad. Homes and businesses have been seized, life savings raided, family heirlooms taken. When those targeted had little inside Iran themselves, the authorities went after their family members back home, interviews show. As the Najafiragheb family pressed their case with the authorities, Mehrnoush said, they encountered dozens of other people facing the specter of losing their life’s savings as punishment for the actions of their relatives abroad. “We realized we weren’t alone,” Ms. Najafiragheb recalled her mother telling her. She said her sister Noushin had declined to be interviewed to avoid further government pressure on her family.

items.title: In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman U.S. officials say is a Chinese spy has drawn attention to the role of intimate relationships in espionage.
items.full_text: At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person. Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.” Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom. It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms. Mr. Huang has acknowledged that he had an affair with Ms. Huang . President Trump has said that Mr. Huang told him that he was not aware that the woman was a spy. China has rejected the espionage allegations against Ms. Huang, calling them smears against the country. U.S. officials have not provided evidence for their claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Israel’s Arrest of Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Raises Concerns
items.summary: Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was detained without being charged with a crime, raising concerns that the domestic security service is overstepping its authority.
items.full_text: Abed Abu Shehadeh, a 38-year-old journalist and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, said he was putting on his pajamas on the evening of Nov. 3 when police officers and intelligence agents burst into his family’s third-floor apartment in Jaffa. They strip-searched him, confiscated his phone, allowed him to dress and then whisked him away, he said in an interview at a restaurant in the city. Five days later, after interrogations by Israel’s domestic security agency, the Shin Bet, Mr. Abu Shehadeh, who lives with his wife and two young children, was let go. A former elected member of the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Council, Mr. Abu Shehadeh has not been charged with a crime. The Israeli authorities have not publicly offered a reason for his arrest, though court records reviewed by The New York Times show that he was accused of being in contact with an unnamed “foreign agent.” His highly publicized arrest — a week after Israel’s national elections — came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have claimed that foreign actors illegally funneled large amounts of money to bribe Arab citizens to vote for Arab political parties. Critics say that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the record gains by Arab parties in the Parliament, or the Knesset, by contending without basis that Arab voters stole the election . items.title: Tourists Brave a Muddy Jungle Trek to See a Famed World War II Wreck
items.summary: Seven Chinese tourists, a dozen villagers and a couple of journalists forded streams and bushwhacked to the downed plane of Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral. Machetes proved handy.
items.full_text: Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams. We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell. Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea. The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943. Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance. items.title: Indonesia’s Vice President, Gibran, Resigns
items.summary: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who is stepping down amid a scandal over his academic credentials, was a symbol of the partnership that elevated President Prabowo Subianto into office.
items.full_text: The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy. Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office. “The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname. Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket. The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence. “From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia. items.title: U.S. Efforts to Tighten Blockade of Iran Rely on Reluctant Neighbors
items.summary: Washington wants to intensify its economic pressure campaign on Iran by closing its land borders. Neighboring states, fearing economic fallout, are pushing back.
items.full_text: The first step in the United States’ campaign to economically strangle Iran was a naval blockade of its ports, cutting off Iranian trade by sea. Next came a raft of new sanctions, grounding much of the country’s air transport network. Now, the United States is going after Iran’s last economic artery: its land routes. Only there, Washington has hit upon a problem. For weeks, U.S. officials have tried — and failed — to diplomatically pressure Iran’s neighbors into shuttering their border crossings, according to three Iraqi officials and one U.S. official with knowledge of the talks, who requested anonymity to speak candidly. Those neighboring states, primarily Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan, are increasingly wary and disgruntled by U.S. policies they say could hurt them as much as Tehran. So, on Saturday, the U.S. military joined the effort, announcing Task Force Iron Gate , which it says will work on “preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.” It is unclear how the task force will operate in practice, and it is unusual for such an economic and security campaign to be run by U.S. Central Command, known as Centcom, which oversees military operations in the Middle East. items.title: Seeking to Broaden Ukraine Talks, U.S. Urges Russia to Include Europe
items.summary: As a round of negotiations ended in Abu Dhabi, President Trump’s envoys said they would go to Moscow as the Kremlin demands discussions on European security structures.
items.full_text: The first round of Ukraine peace talks in nine months ended in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday without a Russian agreement to include Europe in negotiations that have extended, at Moscow’s insistence, to questions of huge consequence for European nations’ security. The two days of talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in the United Arab Emirates were led by President Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. On Thursday, the two Americans are scheduled to meet with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in Moscow and then with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine in Dublin. The Americans said on Wednesday that they would work to nail down the details of what Mr. Kushner billed as the largest humanitarian swap of the war. The envoys are also trying to secure agreement from Moscow to widen the talks to include Europeans, after negotiators in Abu Dhabi discussed Russia’s demands to overhaul European security structures. Reiterating a longstanding European position, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, the European Union’s executive arm, said this week that a cease-fire must come before such discussions. That sequencing would avoid negotiating at gunpoint and test Russian compliance with any agreements. But Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff, trying to find a path forward after nearly two years of fruitless peacemaking efforts, are pushing to grant Moscow its wish of negotiating the postwar security posture in Europe alongside discussions about a cease-fire and territory in Ukraine. items.title: Workers in Spain Stage a General Strike for the First Time in 14 Years
items.summary: Workers in a wide range of industries walked off the job to protest rising rents and stagnant wages, which have become central issues in the campaign.
items.full_text: Spanish workers staged a general strike on Wednesday for the first time in 14 years, protesting the rising rents and stagnant wages that have become central issues in the national election to be held this month. Unions said millions of workers participated in the walkout, while hundreds of thousands of Spaniards joined rallies in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and other cities in the evening. Early on Wednesday, protesters blocked roads in Madrid, set up picket lines outside major factories in Catalonia and disrupted transportation across Spain. Police officers wielding shields and batons forced hundreds of demonstrators away from the Gran Vía, the central thoroughfare in Madrid, which rally goers had blocked. The anger of protesters in the capital was directed largely at “rentistas” — a Spanish term for people who live off rental income. Later in the day, during a march through central Madrid that drew 120,000 protesters according to the government, demonstrators chanted in a festive mood, “One jump, two jumps, whoever doesn’t jump is a rentista.” Clashes with the police erupted in Barcelona, where a group of masked protesters broke away from the crowd after the demonstration ended, according to local news media . The group smashed several shop windows, threw pyrotechnic devices at police officers and tried unsuccessfully to storm an Apple Store, the reports said. items.title: Who Is Colette Kress, the Interim Nvidia CEO Replacing Jensen Huang?
items.summary: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013.
items.full_text: Colette Kress, a longtime Nvidia executive, was appointed by the board of directors as the interim chief executive officer. Nvidia veteran : Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013. She has worked closely with Mr. Huang as the company transitioned from a niche maker of graphics processors used for video games to a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. She previously worked for Cisco and Microsoft. She has an undergraduate degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a M.B.A. from Southern Methodist University. She will remain the company’s finance chief while serving as interim chief executive. Closeness to Jensen Huang : Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Mr. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role. “I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Jensen said in a podcast appearance this year. China : During her time as chief financial officer, Ms. Kress expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China. In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20 to 25 percent of the company’s data center revenue. In addition to lost sales, she has said the policies risk strengthening Nvidia’s competitors in China. Liaison to Wall Street : As chief financial officer, one of Ms. Kress’s main responsibilities was communicating with Wall Street and Nvidia’s investors. On quarterly earnings calls, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message as Nvidia’s revenue and stock price soared. In 2013, Nvidia’s sales were $4.28 billion. In the most recent fiscal year, its annual sales reached $215.9 billion. Personal Wealth : Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price. She owned roughly 4.44 million shares, according to Nvidia’s most recent annual report, worth about $772 million.

items.title: Here’s the latest.
items.full_text: In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce. Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him. The company’s 10-member board said in a statement that Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, would serve as interim chief executive until a permanent successor to Mr. Huang is named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates. Mr. Huang’s exit opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. Over three decades, Mr. Huang, 63, built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of the A.I. projects driving the U.S. economy — and are at the center of the U.S.-China tussle for dominance in A.I. A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who goes by Alice Huang, who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang, and that President Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment. Though Nvidia had said that it had “no reason to believe” that Mr. Huang had compromised national security or company secrets, its board, with a track record of deference to its celebrity C.E.O., opened an investigation. The company’s share price plunged in after-hours trading on Wednesday as the board met to consider Mr. Huang’s future, and continued to slide on Thursday . China has rejected the espionage claims. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. China’s embassy has called the allegations “smears.” Here’s what else to know: A second affair: Mr. Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Read more › C.E.O.’s influence: Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Mr. Huang over Mr. Trump’s approach to A.I. and China. He persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China, and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom project. Trump’s response: Mr. Trump has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, calling him an “honorable man” and saying that Mr. Huang had told him he was not aware that Ms. Huang was an intelligence operative for Beijing. The president is scheduled to travel to China next week , and he said on Monday that he did not plan to bring the Nvidia matter up in talks with China’s leader, Xi Jinping. Closeness to Jensen Huang : Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Mr. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role. “I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Jensen said in a podcast appearance this year. China : During her time as chief financial officer, Ms. Kress expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China. In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20 to 25 percent of the company’s data center revenue. In addition to lost sales, she has said the policies risk strengthening Nvidia’s competitors in China. Liaison to Wall Street : As chief financial officer, one of Ms. Kress’s main responsibilities was communicating with Wall Street and Nvidia’s investors. On quarterly earnings calls, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message as Nvidia’s revenue and stock price soared. In 2013, Nvidia’s sales were $4.28 billion. In the most recent fiscal year, its annual sales reached $215.9 billion. Personal Wealth : Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price. She owned roughly 4.44 million shares, according to Nvidia’s most recent annual report, worth about $772 million. The company’s board named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive. With the change in Nvidia’s leadership, investors face uncertainty about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade and how the problems inside one of the technology industry’s most important companies could affect the broader economy. The fallout could be seen in markets around the world, although the effects appeared limited. Major market indexes in Asia, where many of Nvidia’s partners and rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are based, mostly declined. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell more than 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent. European stock indexes, which are less heavily exposed to A.I., mostly rose on Thursday. But shares in the region’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell more than 2 percent. In the United States, futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped less than 1 percent in premarket trading. The stocks of Nvidia’s fellow tech giants, members of an exclusive club known as the “ Magnificent Seven ,” were little changed. Shares in some of Nvidia’s U.S. rivals were set to climb: AMD rose more than 2 percent and Broadcom gained nearly 2 percent in premarket trading on Thursday. The broader S&P 500 index was set to open slightly lower. Trading outside of official market hours is often choppy, which can exaggerate moves in stock prices. Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the A.I. boom, which has helped to drive U.S. stock markets to new highs in recent years. Nvidia’s board deliberations came after revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Some market analysts covering Nvidia have begun to downgrade their forecasts for the company’s stock. Though the chipmaker is expected to remain a critical part of the A.I. build-out, some noted rising concerns about the company’s governance and lack of a clear succession plan. They argued that these revelations have fundamentally changed Mr. Huang’s position in the tech world and it was unclear what the implications of a change in his role at Nvidia could be. Analysts at Bernstein downgraded Nvidia and sharply lowered their target for its share price. “Our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here,” they wrote. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.” Analysts at RBC Capital Markets also slashed their forecast for the stock, citing the lack of formal succession plan for the chief executive position. “Whether any individual can replicate Huang’s singular combination of technical vision, ecosystem-building acumen and ability to serve as the global face of the A.I. revolution remains an open question,” they noted. Other analysts, including those at Wells Fargo and Mizuho, maintained their bullish views on Nvidia, but said it was increasingly likely that Mr. Huang might not be chief executive for much longer. Nvidia’s stock is down about a third from its peak at the start of October, putting the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high. Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024 , exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500. Analysts still expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A.I. data centers . During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest public company. items.title: Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Megaspeed Investigation
items.summary: In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.
items.full_text: Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang . Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government. In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had been uncooperative. Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe. Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.” “Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said. Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment. During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.” She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.

items.title: Wall Street Sees the Writing on the Wall for Jensen Huang
items.summary: The company’s board is weighing the fate of its chief executive. Silicon Valley and Washington are steeling themselves for life without him.
items.full_text: Andrew here. Put yourself in the shoes of Nvidia’s board: Would you fire Jensen Huang ? An affair with a customer who U.S. intelligence officials determined was a spy for China, as well as what The Times reported was a relationship with an employee, would typically be grounds for removal. At best, these scandals are a distraction. At worst, they make managing the nearly $4 trillion chipmaker virtually impossible, especially if credible evidence emerges that Huang knew about Nvidia chips improperly going to China. Yet does his centrality to the company and the A.I. industry mean overlooking those issues? Elon Musk wrote that he would be honored to hire Huang. Palmer Luckey of Anduril declared , “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in.” The venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote , “We should demand loyalty and accountability, but sainthood cannot be the price of admission to leadership.” Does the Nvidia board have any middle ground? Could Huang step down to become chief technology officer — or is that just window dressing? We should know the answer soon. More below. Huge shoes to fill A month ago, Jensen Huang was firmly ensconced atop Nvidia. Now Silicon Valley — and Wall Street and Washington — are starting to imagine life without him running the giant chipmaker. If Nvidia’s board removes Huang as C.E.O., it would be a sea change at the central cog of the artificial intelligence boom, with wide-ranging consequences, Sri Muppidi and Michael de la Merced report. The latest: Nvidia’s board has met to discuss Huang’s future , after The Times reported that he had an affair with a direct report, Kimberly Powell , as well as with Alice Huang , an executive who U.S. intelligence officials determined is a spy for China. (The Wall Street Journal suggests that his ouster is on the table .) Alice Huang is now living in Beijing , with the knowledge of Chinese security officials, Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources. What Nvidia without Huang as C.E.O. might look like: Remember that the company has no clear succession plan . Analysts have speculated that Colette Kress , its C.F.O. and perhaps its next most prominent executive, could become interim C.E.O. (Nvidia has hired an outside firm to consider possible replacements for Huang, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.) Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Nvidia Shares Plummet as Board Considers Jensen Huang’s Future as CEO
items.summary: News that the chipmaker’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down drove Nvidia’s stock down and reverberated across global markets.
items.full_text: Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang , stepped down from his role. Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 11 percent in premarket trading, extending a drop that is set to wipe roughly $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The company’s board named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive. With the change in Nvidia’s leadership, investors face uncertainty about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade and how the problems inside one of the technology industry’s most important companies could affect the broader economy. The fallout could be seen in markets around the world, although the effects appeared limited. Major market indexes in Asia, where many of Nvidia’s partners and rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are based, mostly declined. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell more than 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent. European stock indexes, which are less heavily exposed to A.I., mostly rose on Thursday. But shares in the region’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell more than 2 percent. items.title: Data Centers Will Continue to Be Built, Despite Midterm Elections
items.summary: Big technology companies saw the tide turn against their giant A.I. projects, but they have the means to weather delays.
items.full_text: Many of the largest technology companies weren’t prepared for the opposition to data centers that has swept the country over the last year. To placate critics, the companies walked back secrecy arrangements , offered greater benefits to local communities and said they would pay more for electricity . It didn’t matter. Even elected officials who had once welcomed the giant data centers, which tech companies are building for their artificial intelligence work, were turning against them. The election swung harder against data centers than polls predicted. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Still there are early signs that the Blue Wave that brought Democrats to power around the country will not send data center construction — and with it the U.S. economy — off a cliff. One analysis, from the investment bank Bernstein, estimated that in the most extreme scenario, 9 percent of projects that would have probably been built will no longer break ground. More realistically, they said, only 2 to 4 percent of future data centers will be canceled nationwide. Another analysis, from Susquehanna Financial Group, predicted that even if some projects die, more data centers for training A.I. will still be built in 2027 and 2028 than this year. “We are not going to see a dramatic downturn,” said Austin Keyser, a top regional official at the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers who advised Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic governor-elect. She campaigned on establishing moratoriums on data center projects that don’t meet certain criteria, such as hiring union workers and building on former industrial sites, not farmland. items.title: Help! A Broken Toilet Grounded My Plane, and the Airline Won’t Cover a Hotel.
items.summary: Turkish Airlines tried to wiggle out of paying for a passenger’s $512 overnight stay after a stomach-churning malfunction forced it to cancel a flight in Denver.
items.full_text: Dear Tripped Up, On May 30, my wife and I were scheduled to take Turkish Airlines’ evening flight from Denver to Istanbul. The flight was delayed several hours because of what we were told was a mechanical problem. We boarded the aircraft at around 11:30 p.m., taxied to the runway and then returned to the gate. The flight was finally canceled at around 1 a.m. Gate agents advised us that no hotel vouchers were available and that we should find hotels and submit our receipts to the airline. We stayed at the airport Westin, paying $512, including taxes and breakfast, and flew out the next day. We heard — and later read in The Denver Post — that the cancellation had been caused by an overflowing lavatory. But the airline sent us a message attributing the disruption to “force majeure,” which to me means an earthquake or a war or something similar. I called the airline and was told to submit my hotel receipts online, which I did twice, but got no response. Turkish Airlines’ customer service plan says the carrier pays for hotels only if the reason for the cancellation was under its control. Is Turkish evading responsibility with this “force majeure” argument? Can you help? Neal, Broomfield, Colo. Dear Neal, How an airline describes the cause of a cancellation can directly affect whether it will cover passengers’ lodging, transportation and meals. For mechanical issues, the answer is often yes; for weather or air-traffic issues, it’s almost always no. U.S. regulations define those categories, but they do not require airlines to pay for stranded passengers’ expenses. Nevertheless, all the major U.S. carriers except Frontier explicitly promise hotel stays in their customer service plans if the reason for the disruption is under their control. The Turkish Airlines policy for U.S. flights is a bit looser — but the airline usually offers lodging for controllable disruptions. For the last couple of years, I’ve kept a file of emails from travelers who suspected, as you do, that a carrier had weaseled its way out of covering passengers’ expenses by misrepresenting what happened. I had avoided the ever-expanding file because I knew that proving the precise cause of any one incident was most likely a fool’s errand. Disruptions can have multiple causes, and the U.S. Department of Transportation gives the airlines flexibility in determining the main one. For example, if a mechanical problem causes a delay, then a storm moves in and shuts down the airport, airlines can blame the weather. No hotel voucher for you! But the evidence in your case seemed pretty overwhelming. When airlines cite force majeure, they are generally referring to extraordinary circumstances beyond their control — like a natural disaster. The Denver Post article had the headline “Turkish Airlines Cancels Flight From Denver Airport After Urine and Feces Erupt From Plane’s Toilet,” which is disgusting but hardly earthquake-level terrible. Citing force majeure seemed like, at best, an entertaining error or, at worst, an attempt to avoid compensating passengers for their hotels, a promise you said gate agents made at the time. items.title: Want to Short a Stock? Kalshi and C.T.F.C. Allow It as ‘Perpetual Trades.’
items.summary: After a federal regulator allowed wagering on stocks and cryptocurrencies, two powerful trading clearinghouses filed lawsuits saying traders would not be properly protected.
items.full_text: In late April, Kalshi, the world’s largest prediction market, invited a big crowd to a posh event to launch a new type of trading that would allow customers to wager on cryptocurrencies they did not own. This type of trading had never before been permitted in the United States. But Kalshi was so confident that it would win approval from its regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, that it booked the event before it had even put in its formal application. After all, the agency’s chairman, Michael S. Selig, had repeatedly signaled that he was a prediction markets booster. When the C.F.T.C. did not move fast enough, Kalshi was forced to cancel the gathering at a glass-domed Brooklyn penthouse with sweeping views of the Manhattan skyline. And the firm’s chief executive, Tarek Mansour, called Mr. Selig to complain, according to three people with knowledge of the call who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation. But Kalshi just needed to be patient. Mr. Selig’s support was never in question. In a series of decisions from May onward, he reversed years of agency policy and gave Kalshi what it wanted: permission to let customers bet on the prices of individual stocks, cryptocurrencies or other assets without buying them or being forced to settle up by a specific date. Now, for example, clients could simply wager that the price of shares of ExxonMobil would fall and then get paid if it did. It was the first time the trades, called perpetuals, were permitted to be offered to American customers. And the agency’s authorizations immediately infuriated officials at some of the nation’s largest trading exchanges who saw Kalshi as a privileged new competitor. Two powerful clearinghouses — the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Cboe Global Markets — have filed suit against the agency, claiming that giving prediction markets this leeway violates federal laws designed to protect investors from insider trading, market manipulation and other abuses. items.title: Tech Giants Invest in German Robotics Start-Up at $8.5 Billion Valuation
items.summary: Agile Robots plans to expand in the United States and increase production in Europe after raising funds in a round led by SoftBank.
items.full_text: Agile Robots, a German company developing industrial robots powered by artificial intelligence, has raised $500 million in new funding from investors including SoftBank and Nvidia that values the start-up at $8.5 billion. The investment will allow Agile to expand in the United States, increase production in Germany and move into new markets — ahead of a potential future initial public offering, said Zhaopeng Chen, Agile’s founder. The company is working with partners including Google DeepMind and has raised a total of $2 billion. Agile is among a crop of fast-growing companies combining artificial intelligence and robotics to help factories increase productivity and lower costs. Developing humanoids and other robots that can carry out more complex tasks in the physical world is critical in Europe, which is trying to narrow an A.I. gap with the United States and China and revive its struggling industries. “Physical A.I. is one of the solutions for Europe,” said Mr. Chen, who started the company in Germany in 2018 after studying engineering in China and completing his doctorate at the German Aerospace Center. Agile’s valuation puts the start-up on par with European companies including Quantum Systems, the German defense technology company valued at $8 billion in July, and Wayve , the British autonomous driving company valued at $8.6 billion in February. Neura Robotics, a German company that has raised funds from companies including Nvidia, Amazon and the cryptocurrency company Tether, was valued at about $7 billion after raising as much as $1.4 billion.

items.title: Nvidia’s Stock Price Plummets as Board Is Said to Consider Jensen Huang’s Future as CEO
items.summary: News of the board’s deliberations about Jensen Huang’s job drove Nvidia’s stock down more than 8 percent in after-hours trading.
items.full_text: Nvidia’s share price plummeted in after-hours trading on Wednesday, as the company’s board considered the future of the chief executive, Jensen Huang, a decision that could reverberate across global markets. News of the board’s deliberations drove Nvidia’s stock down more than 8 percent late Wednesday, a move that would erase hundreds of billions of dollars in market value if the drop persisted into the official open of trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. Trading after the market is closed can be thin, which can exaggerate moves in individual stock prices. Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the artificial intelligence boom, which has helped to drive the stock market to repeated new highs in recent years. The board’s deliberations on Wednesday follow revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. With the leadership of Nvidia in doubt, Wall Street faced new uncertainty about the A.I. trade and how the problems inside one of the world’s most important companies could affect the broader economy. Nvidia’s stock is now down about a third from its peak at the start of October, a decline worth more than $1.5 trillion in market value. The sharp fall put the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high. Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024 , exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the S&P 500. The rapid run-up in Nvidia’s share price put it at the forefront of an exclusive club of tech giants known as the “ Magnificent Seven ,” that had fueled the stock market’s gains in recent years. Analysts expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A.I. data centers . During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest company. Including Wednesday’s after-hours decline, the company’s shares have lost roughly 15 percent of their value this year.

items.title: Nvidia Scandal Puts Lori Huang, Jensen Huang’s Wife, In the Spotlight
items.summary: Lori Huang, who has been married to the Nvidia chief executive for more than 40 years, stands out among tech titan spouses for how private she has been.
items.full_text: In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce. Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him. By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background. For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion. By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight. That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy . In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight. The bombshell news had implications for U.S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A.I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market. items.title: Silicon Valley Tech Allies Support Jensen Huang
items.summary: Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures cast the Nvidia chief’s relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse, not a security failure.
items.full_text: Within hours of Jensen Huang’s admission on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors closed ranks around him. Their messages, delivered mostly on social media, were consistent. Mr. Huang’s relationship with a woman identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese spy was a personal failing. Losing the Nvidia chief executive, they argued, would be a far bigger blow to the country, and America couldn’t win the artificial intelligence race without him. “Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in a post on Sunday afternoon . He said that Mr. Huang “did something incredibly dumb,” and that it was bad for America, “but my guess is there was no bad intention.” He concluded that Mr. Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post and added: “I agree.” The show of loyalty reflects Mr. Huang’s rarefied standing in Silicon Valley. In the three decades since he co-founded Nvidia, he has gone from running a maker of video game graphics cards to presiding over the company at the center of the A.I. boom, now one of the world’s most valuable companies. Nvidia’s chips are the scarce resource every A.I. company needs, a position that makes Mr. Huang something of a kingmaker. Decisions about who gets his products, and how many, can shape which start-ups and tech giants pull ahead. Nvidia’s finances are also deeply intertwined with other leading A.I. companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic . (China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.) Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: This Trader Raised Alarm About Nvidia’s China Entanglements Months Ago
items.summary: Christian Lamarco, a 31-year-old short seller and trader, warned about financial and personal problems at Nvidia in May.
items.full_text: Early on May 13, Christian Lamarco, a little-known stock researcher and trader, could barely sleep. Shortly after dawn the 31-year-old would release what amounted to the magnum opus of his career: A 40-page exposé on questionable behavior at Nvidia. The report mostly comprised a sober examination of whether the chipmaker was being honest about the scale of its China business. But at the top of Page 3, Mr. Lamarco tucked in a paragraph-long warning of the “uncomfortably close relationship” between Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, and Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a huge customer. Mr. Lamarco says his interest in their relationship had been piqued by reporting in The New York Times and Bloomberg News that first detailed a year ago how the Nvidia chief executive and Ms. Huang were seen together socializing with other tech executives in Asia. So Mr. Lamarco started digging around for himself, using paid expert networks — middlemen that connect investors with company insiders — to chat with current and former Megaspeed and Nvidia employees about Ms. Huang and the companies’ business. The employees wondered about what Mr. Lamarco months ago termed “special” ties between the two executives. But almost no one noticed his report . Nvidia’s stock rose that day in May when Mr. Lamarco’s findings were released online. Among the little feedback, he recalled this week, was one note calling him developmentally disabled and another warning him to “watch out.” Now, the 31-year-old looks prescient. Mr. Huang, after a series of forceful denials, this weekend confessed to an extramarital affair with Ms. Huang, who U.S. intelligence has accused of being a Chinese spy. items.title: Who Is Alice Huang, the Woman in the Middle of Nvidia’s Spy Scandal?
items.summary: Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset, emerged from the high-flying world of Shanghai finance to work with tech titans and obtain essential A.I. chips.
items.full_text: In December 2023, a Chinese executive who goes by Alice Huang met with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, and a small group of colleagues at an Italian restaurant in Singapore. In a photo of the previously unreported meeting, which was confirmed by The New York Times, Ms. Huang smiled as she posed next to Mr. Huang, who was in his trademark black leather jacket. He held a glass of red wine. For Ms. Huang, there was reason to celebrate. Backed by wealthy investors in Shanghai, she had just restructured a company that would soon buy billions of dollars in Nvidia artificial intelligence chips. The U.S. government had barred Chinese companies from buying the advanced chips, but Ms. Huang had sidestepped this prohibition by creating a firm, Megaspeed, through a Singaporean shell company. Her close relationship with Nvidia’s leader also appeared to smooth the way. Four days after the ownership change Megaspeed was named a Nvidia cloud partner, giving it access to the coveted components. Their relationship is now at the center of a global geopolitical competition between China and the U.S. government to dominate A.I. It has also shaken and captivated the tech industry on both sides of the Pacific, surfacing often invisible details of the fierce technological race, like spy craft and the human vulnerabilities of A.I. kingmakers like Mr. Huang. The meeting in Singapore was a sign of how Ms. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Huang goes back further than previously known. It also speaks to the close social and business ties that grew during years of tech collaboration between China and the United States, and how they have persisted despite the icy geopolitical divide of the past decade. items.title: Here’s the latest.
items.summary: The chief executive has been under scrutiny for an affair with a woman said to be a Chinese spy, as well as for a relationship with a subordinate at his A.I. chip company. Nvidia’s finance chief, Colette Kress, was named interim leader.
items.full_text: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, resigned on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with an executive who reported to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese spy. The chip company’s 10-member board met for several hours Wednesday evening and agreed to name Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive, until a permanent successor has been named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia also appointed Harvey Jones, a longtime tech entrepreneur and investor, as the chip company’s chairman. In a statement, Mr. Jones said that the board was confident in Ms. Kress and the executive team and that it expected “the company’s operations, customer commitments and product road map to continue without interruption.” Mr. Huang’s exit opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. The Silicon Valley firm is a linchpin of the A.I. boom and one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. That dominance has made Mr. Huang one of the world’s wealthiest people, as well as an ally of President Trump’s. Mr. Trump was previously informed about Mr. Huang’s relationship with the woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset but took no action. He has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, saying he was an “honorable man” who did not know the woman was a Chinese agent. Few Silicon Valley executives — with the possible exception of Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, and Steve Jobs of Apple — have been as synonymous with their companies as Mr. Huang, 63. He was a founder of Nvidia in 1993. He manages all aspects of its business as chief executive, and his family members have steadily risen through the company’s ranks. With a 3.56 percent stake, he is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder. He has had such a tight grip on the company that there is no clear successor. items.title: Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him
items.summary: Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, is already facing scrutiny over an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.
items.full_text: Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company. The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct , employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates. Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video. Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people. Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset. This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang . China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

items.title: Court Rules That Sexual Harassment Case Against SpaceX Can Proceed
items.summary: The company had argued that the case, involving eight former workers, must be resolved before an arbitrator.
items.full_text: A federal appeals court ruled Tuesday that a sexual harassment lawsuit brought by eight former employees of the rocket company SpaceX can proceed in court. The company had attempted to shift the case to a private arbitration process, arguing that the plaintiffs had signed agreements requiring that move. But the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concluded that the case could proceed under a federal law that allows plaintiffs in sexual harassment cases to sue in court even if they’ve signed arbitration agreements. Tom Moline, one of the former workers, said in a statement, “The Ninth Circuit correctly recognized SpaceX’s claims for what they are: an attempt to hide and distract from the toxic culture of sexual harassment and retaliation that persists to this day.” SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The case dates back to a letter the employees wrote and circulated within the company in 2022, in which they urged SpaceX to separate itself from social media comments made by Elon Musk, the company’s founder and chief executive, including one in which he poked fun at sexual harassment accusations against him. The company fired five employees shortly after, and four more employees over the next few months. In many instances, the company cited the employees’ role in producing and distributing the letter when firing them. A top company official also told several of them that they had wasted large amounts of company time on the letter. Eight of the nine employees filed charges with the National Labor Relations Board, arguing that the company had violated their federally protected right to engage in collective activity at work. The employees also later filed a lawsuit in California with several accusations from some or all members of the group, including claims that the company had illegally retaliated against them and failed to prevent harassment. The labor board eventually dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, while SpaceX successfully moved the California case to federal court. Once there, the company argued that the employees had signed agreements requiring them to pursue the case before an arbitrator. But a Federal District Court ruled last year that the case could proceed under the federal law that allows plaintiffs in sexual harassment cases to avoid arbitration. A three-judge panel on the appeals court, by a 2-to-1 margin, affirmed that ruling on Tuesday. SpaceX can now ask the full appeals court to reconsider the case. If it doesn’t, or if the court denies the company’s request, the case will go back before the district court judge.

items.title: Trump Officials Clashed Over Megaspeed, Firm at Heart of Nvidia Affair
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week about why the administration had not put restrictions on advanced chip sales to Megaspeed.
items.full_text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week over his handling of a Singaporean company at the heart of revelations about Chinese spying on Nvidia, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned sales of advanced A.I. chips to the firm. The exchange, which took place at the White House on Thursday and was described by people briefed on it, highlighted growing tensions inside the Trump administration over A.I. policy in general and the Commerce Department’s posture toward Nvidia in particular. The internal debate has only intensified after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, acknowledged he had an affair with a woman who had helped lead the Singaporean data center company, Megaspeed. The woman, Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, has been identified by U.S. intelligence as a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported . Mr. Lutnick responded to Mr. Bessent that the Commerce Department could now move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place, said the people briefed on the exchange, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the discussions were private. A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the conversation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had taken place. She said that the decision about whether to add companies to the entity list was an administration-wide one. The Treasury Department did not provide a comment. The United States has imposed restrictions since late 2022 on selling advanced chips directly to China. But Megaspeed and other companies have sidestepped those rules by setting up data centers in Southeast Asia to cater to Chinese clients. U.S. officials have also been investigating Megaspeed for potentially diverting those chips illegally into China, a charge that Megaspeed has denied.
